body.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon murder trial live: Accused continues evidence about deaths of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
Beau Lamarre-Condon is back in the witness box giving evidence in his double murder trial.
He is accused of shooting his former partner, Jesse Baird, and his new boyfriend Luke Davies with his police-issue pistol.
Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty in the NSW Supreme Court.
Follow all the developments.

Discussion whether to throw things out in skip bin
Lamarre-Condon says he wanted to throw out Baird's possessions in a tip, but his male friend, who can't be identified, recommended a skip bin instead.
The pair were getting lunch in Cronulla and Lamarre-Condon claims his friend pointed out a skip bin at local bowls club.
"He got out and told me to chuck" the belongings in there, he says.
"I did return later by myself and I did [throw it there]."
Friend recommended concrete to 'sink' bodies, accused alleges
At this stage, he's saying he never told this friend about shooting Davies.
He denies saying "I couldn't leave a witness".
Lamarre-Condon tells the court he discussed with this friend how to get rid of the bodies.
He claims his friend recommended sinking the bodies in a dam.
He "said to buy concrete ... with sand in it to weigh it down more ... and use counter-weights".
Movements on February 20, 2024
He says on February 20 he moved Baird's belongings into the rental van.
On this day, he also went to Balmain Police Station to get a radio battery.
While he was there, he scribbled over a return date for his gun from the original date of the 18th to February 20.
He says he had moved the bodies the day before, on February 19.
Lamarre-Condon is describing a conversation with another friend where he says he told her what happened, and she told him not to report it.
We're still on February 20 and he says he returned the gun to Miranda Police Station and picked up the friend who he went to on the day of the alleged murders.
He denies saying "pew pew", calling it something "a kid would say".
Van rental on day of alleged murders
The accused is talking about a message to a friend saying "I should win an Oscar, hey".
He says this is a code to "see if he would know" if it was his friend, not his brother.
On February 19, he's talking about reserving a van at 7:39pm.
"I think I put it down for 9pm ... This van that was after the incident occurred was solely for getting Jesse and Luke out the courtyard from the property."
He also took his mattress to a lane, and moved Baird's belongings back into his room.
Accused 'threw knife' outside house
On Tuesday, February 20 he went back and tried to remove the bullet from the door.
He's making a pushing motion and describing trying to jam a screwdriver into the door to push the bullet out.
He took the bullet and "threw it somewhere". He can't say where he put it and doesn't "remember".
In relation to the knife, he "threw it" where his car was park.
"Because at this point ... I was about 90 per cent sure that I wasn't going to go to police at this stage," he says.
Trip to Bunnings and return to terrace
Lamarre-Condon went to Bunnings in Alexandria thinking about the door he needed to replace. He bought a tool bag and cleaning products.
The accused told a friend he had "rolled his ankle" and cancelled dinner plans that night.
He returned to the sharehouse and cleaned the kitchen "and put Jesse and Luke in surfboard bags".
In relation to Baird's phone, he says he sent messages from it "later that night".
"I was planning to send it to my friend [in Perth] ... and I ultimately decided against that."It wasn't right."
"I was planning to send it to my friend [in Perth] ... and I ultimately decided against that.
Lamarre-Condon says it would be a 'death wish' inside jail
It wasn't until the Wednesday when Lamarre-Condon says it hit him that it was "real".

"In my mind I was fearful if I went to police I knew what I had done to Jesse ... was manslaughter."If I did the right thing I would sign a death wish ... I was going to be killed ... because of the uniform I wear and we put people in jail."
"In my mind I was fearful if I went to police I knew what I had done to Jesse ... was manslaughter.
"If I did the right thing I would sign a death wish ... I was going to be killed ... because of the uniform I wear and we put people in jail."
He says he thought he'd be believed "somewhat" but then was concerned he might not be.
Accused says he didn't want housemates to see scene
He says the situation did not "feel real" when asked why he didn't go to police.
He says he didn't want Baird's housemates to see the scene if it was "real".

"It felt like I was detached from my body ... this isn't real, but if it real the housemates ... are going to be traumatised."You need to figure out if it's real, and if it is, you need to get the bodies out the house and then go to the police."
"It felt like I was detached from my body ... this isn't real, but if it real the housemates ... are going to be traumatised.
"You need to figure out if it's real, and if it is, you need to get the bodies out the house and then go to the police."
Plan to buy a suitcase
Continuing on about what he told his friend, he says he told him "there was someone else there".
He says he told him he "didn't shoot the second person" and says he asked him where to get a "door from" to replace the one with the bullet hole lodged in.
Lamarre-Condon says he asked his friend to leave work to help him "figure out if it was real or not".
The friend says he could meet him later on, and Lamarre-Condon drove to Miranda Westfield to buy a suitcase or sleeping bag.
He "bought a surfboard bag" instead because he already had one.
What accused told a friend after alleged murders
Lamarre-Condon visited the friend at his workplace in Menai, south of Sydney.
He says he told him he "killed somebody" and emphasised it was singular.
He told him he went to Baird's house to "get my things", "looked for my stuff, heard noises" and "ran upstairs".
In this recollection to a friend he says he thought "nobody was there" and says he told him he "shot Jesse".
He talked about the two shots relating to Baird but didn't tell him about Davies.
Lamarre-Condon told friend 'something's gone horribly wrong'
Lamarre-Condon is describing what he did next.
He says he doesn't know how long he was in the house.
"I must have been in the house for an hour," he says.
He then went to wipe blood from the kitchen, hallway, doorways and in Baird's bedroom.
He wrapped the knife in paper towel.
Then, he went upstairs, got his high-vis jacket and possessions and walked back to the Mazda.

"Things just didn't feel real and I just wanted to talk to anybody, somebody, to validate what I was experiencing was real life or delusion," so he called a friend."Something's gone horribly wrong," he told him.
"Things just didn't feel real and I just wanted to talk to anybody, somebody, to validate what I was experiencing was real life or delusion," so he called a friend.
"Something's gone horribly wrong," he told him.
Lamarre-Condon 'passed out' after deaths
He says he goes back to Baird and yelled at him "please get up" and "don't be dead".
Lamarre-Condon says he had a panic attack and started dissociating and hyperventilating.
"It was like I was floating out of my body and looking down at myself and everything around me didn't seem real," he says.
He says he went to the couch and "passed out for a period of time".
"When I got back up I moved Jesse into the bedroom and I moved Luke further into the bedroom so I could shut the door."
Baird's bedroom mostly 'empty'
After the gun went off, hitting Luke Davies, Lamarre-Condon says he picked up the gun from the ground.
"I remember thinking, 'do not touch the handle of the gun'," he says, immediately holstering it.
He says he checked if Davies was responsive and walked to the entryway to examine the door.
Lamarre-Condon is describing what he saw in Baird's bedroom, which was in the process of being packed up and mostly "empty".
Court resumes
We're back. Lamarre-Condon is picking up his evidence in the witness box.
He was at times emotional describing the events of February 19, 2024 and had rosary beads wrapped around his hand.
Morning tea break
The jury is taking a short break for morning tea.
We'll continue live blogging Lamarre-Condon's testimony when they return.
Phone no longer working
After the gun went off, Lamarre-Condon says the phone dropped and hit the ground.
He says the phone was no longer "operating" upon impact.
He noticed the bedroom door was "flung open" and the "hole that punctured" with the bullet lodged in still.
"I looked at the phone and picked it up ... and it was inoperable and had a crack on the screen."
Davies's death as gun discharged again
He says at this point the two are outside Baird's bedroom in the hallway.
The bullet went through his head and through the door, he says.
The impact flung the door open and happened "so, so quick".
He says Davies's finger was on the trigger.
Accused pivots Davies away from him
"I was in the surrender position ... I got up from the floor and I moved Luke's arm."
He's describing his left hand grabbing Davies's wrist and turning it away.
He pivots Davies's wrist away from him and his right hand is still holding the phone.
He says he's not moving Davies's whole arm, just his wrist "towards himself".
"At that point I was just looking at his firearm ... and I saw ... he was obviously pulling down on the trigger."
The gun went off, Lamarre-Condon says.
Gun towards his head, Lamarre-Condon says
He says he told Davies "please don't shoot me, I'm not here to shoot you" and yells at him to "get out".
"That's when he raised the gun towards my head ... and said 'f*** off'".
He says Davies put his finger on the trigger and that's when his "police training kicked in".
He says he tried to get out the "line of fire", and pivot Davies's wrist "away from me".
The phone, calling 000, is still on his person.
Encounter with Luke Davies
His helmet is still on and visor is still down.
He looks up and "sees someone I don't know", who he now knows to be Luke Davies.
"He was holding my gun he must have picked it up from the living room."It was pointed towards me at my chest, and he says 'I'm going to f***ing shoot you'".
"He was holding my gun he must have picked it up from the living room.
"It was pointed towards me at my chest, and he says 'I'm going to f***ing shoot you'".
He says he puts his hands in the air, lowers his body, and tries to show he's "not a threat".
Triple Zero call from phone in kitchen
He says there was a phone on the kitchen counter and tries to get him 'help'.
He doesn't know whose it is, presses the emergency button and dials Triple Zero (000).
He says the nearest hospital, St Vincent's was a short distance away.
"The thought process was get on the street to flag down" an ambulance."My mindset was call Triple Zero ... and flag someone down who could help."
"The thought process was get on the street to flag down" an ambulance.
"My mindset was call Triple Zero ... and flag someone down who could help."
Lamarre-Condon says he tries to 'save' Baird
"Yanking" the gun with "all my might", it "flies into the living room".
"It went behind me into the other room."
"It went behind me into the other room."
He says he's now laying directly on top of Baird and his ears are "ringing out" and he "can't hear a thing".
He's crying as he recounts when he "realises what has happened".
He sees a wound on his right temple.
"I get up ... I look at Jesse and again I'm now in police mode."What do I do to save him?"
"I get up ... I look at Jesse and again I'm now in police mode.
"What do I do to save him?"
He puts him in the recovery position, he says.
"I thought he was alive."
Lamarre-Condon says he's 'responsible' for Baird's death
Baird dropped the knife and he "grabbed" the firearm, pulling it towards him.

"I still had my finger on the trigger," he says."He falls over and loses his footing ... he's looking to his left ... I'm now falling to the floor with Jesse."As we're falling to the ground I'm yanking the gun and I accidentally discharge the gun."
"I still had my finger on the trigger," he says.
"He falls over and loses his footing ... he's looking to his left ... I'm now falling to the floor with Jesse.
"As we're falling to the ground I'm yanking the gun and I accidentally discharge the gun."
He says it is "my fault" and Baird did not have his finger on the trigger.
"I'm responsible for his death but it wasn't intentional."
The 'split moment second' before shooting
The struggle "felt like eternity" he says, and at one point the knife swung and tore his shirt open.
"At that point, that's when I realised, shit ... I'm going to be dead.
"As police officers we're trained to shoot people at the centre point mass."
He says he didn't want to do this and aimed for his shoulder instead.
"I had a split moment second where I said, drop the knife or I'll shoot you."I was 110 per cent going to have the knife in my throat and I would be dead ... and Jesse Baird would be here instead".
"I had a split moment second where I said, drop the knife or I'll shoot you.
"I was 110 per cent going to have the knife in my throat and I would be dead ... and Jesse Baird would be here instead".
He pulled it out and aimed for his right shoulder and discharged the firearm.
Lamarre-Condon claims he was 'pinned up against wall'
Lamarre-Condon says he called out for Baird to "drop the knife".
He says if he let his arm go and ran out, he would get "stabbed in the back".
"I thought push him out the [back] door with all your might ... slam the door on him and get out the house."I attempted to do that ... but Jesse was too much adrenaline."
"I thought push him out the [back] door with all your might ... slam the door on him and get out the house.
"I attempted to do that ... but Jesse was too much adrenaline."
He says the situation was "heightened and quick" and Baird pushed him up to the corner.
"I was pinned up against the wall ... and Jesse was in front of me with the knife."
He says the knife is near his exposed neck.
Baird lunges at Lamarre-Condon, he says
He's crying in the witness box and wiping tears.
Downstairs, he says he sees the front door shut.
"My firearm was secreted under my shirt, you couldn't see it.
"I could not see anyone in my vicinity."
Looking to the kitchen he says he "saw Jesse".
"He had masking tape in his left hand and a knife in his right hand and he was sealing shut the brown storage box in the kitchen."
He says he looked up and started yelling "we're getting robbed".
"He couldn't see it was me because the visor was down.
"I froze ... he had the knife, he dropped the tape and he lunged at me."
He says he tries to hold Baird back and tells him it's him, not a robber.
He says Baird wasn't processing who it was and says "get f***ed c***".
They're struggling with the knife, he says.
Lamarre-Condon keeps helmet on and hides
At this point, he removes his backpack, high-vis jacket, but kept the helmet on before hiding behind the housemate's bedroom door.
He thought someone might have seen him going up the stairs.
"I could hear downstairs what I thought ... was someone calling the police."I didn't know or interpret it was two people talking to each other."
"I could hear downstairs what I thought ... was someone calling the police.
"I didn't know or interpret it was two people talking to each other."
After a minute or two he heard a "door shut" and thought the person on the phone had left.
Accused runs up the stairs to avoid being seen
"I looked down the hallway and could see another brown storage box towards the kitchen," he says.
In the living room at this point, he says he saw the back door partially open from the kitchen.
"I could hear noises behind the door."As I was hearing sounds ... I saw someone's arm push up against the back door... I immediately ran upstairs to hide."
"I could hear noises behind the door.
"As I was hearing sounds ... I saw someone's arm push up against the back door... I immediately ran upstairs to hide."
He says he didn't leave out the front door because he would be seen.
He goes into Baird's housemate's bedroom.
Lamarre-Condon starts searching for his belongings
He walks back up and plans to knock on the front door, he says.
"I knocked on the front door three times."There was no response."I pushed open the door ... fully and yelled out 'hello' in a loud voice."
"I knocked on the front door three times.
"I pushed open the door ... fully and yelled out 'hello' in a loud voice."
He says he couldn't see anyone inside.
"I saw empty clothing racks ... two storage boxes and two clothing racks.
He says he looked in Baird's bedroom door and saw his room was mostly empty.
Lamarre-Condon says he saw nobody and looked into storage boxes in the hallway for "my belongings"
Front door open when Lamarre-Condon walks up
Lamarre-Condon, with his face covered and in high-vis, walks back towards Baird's sharehouse.
The surfboard cover was left in the Mazda, he says, because he couldn't see Baird's ute which had the surfboard in it.
Last time he checked the phone it was just after 9am, and he thinks he got there about 9:10am.

"I just thought to myself to wait until 9:30," he says " just to be sure he's not there"."I proceeded to walk up and I was intending to go up and knock but as I got up to the street ... I could see his front door was partially open and see multiple items in the doorway."
"I just thought to myself to wait until 9:30," he says " just to be sure he's not there".
"I proceeded to walk up and I was intending to go up and knock but as I got up to the street ... I could see his front door was partially open and see multiple items in the doorway."
This includes furniture items and boxes. He walked away.
Lamarre-Condon discusses the 'moment that caused this'
Lamarre-Condon is talking about seeing the parked motorcycle with a helmet "dangling from the handle" and a delivery bag on the rear.
He also saw a high-vis hooded jacket, waterproof pants and gloves.

"As soon as I saw that I had an idea ... it's this moment here that caused, start, if I didn't do this."I wish I didn't do this but I had the thought process if I put on this ... outfit and look like a delivery driver I would knock on Jesse's door ... and that way I couldn't be accused of harassment.
"As soon as I saw that I had an idea ... it's this moment here that caused, start, if I didn't do this.
"I wish I didn't do this but I had the thought process if I put on this ... outfit and look like a delivery driver I would knock on Jesse's door ... and that way I couldn't be accused of harassment.
He says if Baird opened the door he could claim "wrong address" and if he didn't answer, he could enter safely.
Lamarre-Condon says he put the gear on.
Accused says he couldn't have left police gun in car
He left the share house to get a coffee. He parked and got out the car near Five Ways, Paddington and saw "an Uber Eats motorcycle that was parked".
The gun was on his plain clothes holster he was wearing and "I put it on because you can't leave the gun on your car".
The holster goes on a belt around the waist, he says.
"You can criminally charged for leaving your firearm in the car ... I'd be in a lot of shit," he says.
Confusion whether Baird had home left or not
"I found it unusual Jesse hadn't left for work," he says. It was about 9am at this time.
Baird had been made redundant but had been offered a role at Channel 10.
"I wanted to wait definitely until 9:30 to knock on the door," he says.
He says he couldn't knock on Baird's door in case he "shut the door on his face" and called the police accusing "harassment".
"I was worried if I knocked on the door it would be perceived as harassment and get an AVO."
Search for Baird's ute on day of alleged murders
Lamarre-Condon says he took his mum's car so he could take his belongings back without being recognised.
He picked up the Mazda, a rental, from Zetland, before driving to Paddington just after 6am.
"I was looking for Jesse's ute but I was unaware it was at a mechanic," he says, wanting to see if he was home and also to retrieve his surfboard from the back.
He took Baird's housemate's parking spot.
"I did not want to enter the house if anyone was home."I wanted to be 110 per cent certain" no-one was home, he says.
"I did not want to enter the house if anyone was home.
"I wanted to be 110 per cent certain" no-one was home, he says.
Accused says it was 'just going to be a normal day'
He left the house early on February 19 about 5am.
"I was going to get my belongings back before going to Miranda Police Station" to fill out a form requesting personal leave.
He was going to go about his day, he says, and go out for dinner with a friend.
"It was just going to be a normal day," he says, breaking down into tears.
Suicide ideation night before alleged murders
"This was going to be the night I was either going to return my gun ... or continue driving to the national park without anyone knowing and take my own life," he says.
He says he told his mum about his suicide ideation and she told him he had to leave the force and see a psychiatrist.

"I then finally agreed on the morning of the 19th of February it was time to go off from work," he says."The plan was take time off on stress leave for a couple of months and see how I was feeling on medication."
"I then finally agreed on the morning of the 19th of February it was time to go off from work," he says.
"The plan was take time off on stress leave for a couple of months and see how I was feeling on medication."
Friend to text 'if I don't get to talk to you again'
The car was parked in an unlimited parking spot in Zetland because he says his mum was going to babysit Lamarre-Condon's nephew the following day.
He's being asked about a message he sent a friend before 9pm on February 18.
"If I don't get to talk to you again I just want to let you know I love you so much," he texted her at the time.
"I did send that," he tells the court today.
Lamarre-Condon made dinner plans on day of incident
He says his phone wasn't on airplane mode in the Hertz rental car.
"I never had any intentions to hide my location ... I was actively using my phone," he says.
He says he was making dinner plans on February 19, 2024 - the day of the incident.
Mum urges Lamarre-Condon to 'leave the police force'
He's recounting a conversation with his mum in the car on the way to rent the car.
"I put my phone on airplane mode ... my mum could tell something wasn't right."I had told her I was essentially mentally wasn't feeling okay because of work."
"I put my phone on airplane mode ... my mum could tell something wasn't right.
"I had told her I was essentially mentally wasn't feeling okay because of work."
His mum was a police officer and had "been through serious incidents".
The conversation was picked back up in their Balmain home.
"She was telling me it was time to leave the police force."
Rental car hired for mother day before incident
Lamarre-Condon says he needed to help his mum rent a car the following day.
"She needed a hire care from Mascot," he says."Her car was in for servicing ... in Marrickville on the 19th of February."
"She needed a hire care from Mascot," he says.
"Her car was in for servicing ... in Marrickville on the 19th of February."
He clarifies it was for a repair and remembers the car was leaking.
"At this point she didn't know how long she just had an estimate ... it wasn't clear at the start."She just knew she was taking it in on 19th February, the day of the incident."
"At this point she didn't know how long she just had an estimate ... it wasn't clear at the start.
"She just knew she was taking it in on 19th February, the day of the incident."
Lamarre-Condon took padlock out of gun safe
On February 18, he went back to Balmain Police Station before about 6pm.
"I put the gun in my bag and I retrieved my personal-issue padlock," he says.
He says he was not trying to give the impression he was returning the gun.
"I opened the gun safe to get my padlock back ... I took my gun."
He's disputing he held the door in a certain way to block CCTV.
Accused talks to officer about Lilie James murder at job
On February 18, he retrieved his gun from Balmain for his shift as an officer at a pro-Palestinian march.
He's talking about a conversation with a fellow officer about the murder of Lilie James at a Sydney school.
"I had some pretty general questions," he says, claiming it was the first time he'd heard about it.
Lamarre-Condon talks about new surfboard cover
On Saturday, February 17, 2024 he's talking about getting a surfboard cover at Miranda Westfield.

"I planned to go get my belongings from Jesse's house ... I wanted to retrieve my surfboard from Jesse's ute so I needed to get a cover for that."I needed to get a new surfboard cover" because his old one was "ripped and torn" and discarded.
"I planned to go get my belongings from Jesse's house ... I wanted to retrieve my surfboard from Jesse's ute so I needed to get a cover for that.
"I needed to get a new surfboard cover" because his old one was "ripped and torn" and discarded.
He says he has been surfing since he was 13.
He's talking about a dark sense of humour joke about the surfboard bag being like a "body bag" to his friend at the Decathlon store.
Accused transferred gun to station 'closest to home'
He's being asked why he transferred his gun from Miranda to Balmain.
Lamarre-Condon says he had a "user pay" shift coming up on February 18 for a pro-Palestinian march and it was usual to "keep their firearm at a station closest to their home".
Back to February 16, he took cash out and went on a date, he says.
He can't remember if he stayed at his date's house or went home.
Gun signed out three days before alleged murders
We're now hearing about February 16, 2024 which is three days before the alleged murders.
He signed out a firearm with "permission" and says he got his car washed.
He says he was thinking about getting his belongings back from Baird's on that day but got his car washed in Zetland.
The accused was off-duty and also had his gun on him, before securing his gun at Balmain Police Station.
Friend 'puts idea' into Lamarre-Condon's head about retrieving belongings

After this point at the national park, Lamarre-Condon says he started taking his step dad's medication for depression and anxiety after "really realising the severity and gravity of what I was trying to do to myself".
He's now talking about a "bitter breakup" a friend had with her ex.
She says she was going to go back into his house to get back her belongings while he was not there and "successfully got her belongings back" including a Cartier ring.
He's asked if she "put the idea in" his head.
Lamarre-Condon agrees, saying he "remembered about my Cartier ring, the last time I saw it was the 16th November ... I put it in [Baird's] bedside drawer.
"That ring is $25,000."
Lamarre-Condon fires gun twice in national park
"I fired it a single time at a tree," he says, when asked if he fired the gun.
He says "stuff went in my eyes" when he pulled the trigger.
He fired a second shot through a bag to prevent more material going into his eyes, not to subdue noise.
"Little brown paper bag that is that is never going to change the gun shot," he says."It would be pretty silly to think [the bag] would change the sound of the gun shot."
"Little brown paper bag that is that is never going to change the gun shot," he says.
"It would be pretty silly to think [the bag] would change the sound of the gun shot."
His friend at the time was listening to police radio.
Accused took friend to a national park with gun
On February 1, 2024 he went to the Royal National Park with a friend, and packed his gun.
He says he signed a firearm out from Miranda Police Station after work.
The accused says he had many conversations with this friend of his thoughts of suicide.
"We had multiple conversations but I didn't tell him why we were going there," he says.
He says he didn't want people to hear the gunshot and find his body, so he kept his police radio on to keep track of people in the area.
Lamarre-Condon says his mental health was 'on-and-off'

"Was there ever an agreement ... that your relationship was an exclusive relationship," his barrister asks."... We were doing things couples would be doing ... and it was an intimate relationship but no we were not exclusive, I was still seeing people," he replied.
"Was there ever an agreement ... that your relationship was an exclusive relationship," his barrister asks.
"... We were doing things couples would be doing ... and it was an intimate relationship but no we were not exclusive, I was still seeing people," he replied.
Lamarre-Condon is being asked about his mental health in February 2024, which he describes as "not good".
"My mental state in the entire period I was seeing Jesse ... was on-and-off ... but yes it did decline in February," he says.
He says this was due to stress and bullying or harassment at work and was "actively taking steps to plan my suicide".
Jury and Lamarre-Condon have taken their seats
Lamarre-Condon in back in the witness seat and the jury have taken their place.
He's again wearing a grey suit and black tie, and was swivelling in his chair as he waited for the line of enquiry to kick off.
His barrister, John Stratton SC, is asking about the last time he saw Baird before the shooting.
He says the date was on November 18, 2023.
He's now been shown a still from a video he took of Baird on August 23, 2023 at The Carrington in Surry Hills.
The basics of the case
The trial is now in its seventh week and jurors have heard evidence or statements from around 90 witnesses.
Lamarre-Condon is giving his account of what happened on the day former TV presenter Jesse Baird and Qantas flight attendant Luke Davies died.
The Crown's case is that Lamarre-Condon developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with Baird after a casual romance during parts of 2023.
He's pleaded not guilty and is arguing self-defence, with his lawyers previously telling the jury that the deaths were the result of two separate struggles involving the pistol.
The 31-year-old is accused of shooting the pair with his police pistol in Baird's Paddington share house in February 2024.
Where did we leave off yesterday?
Lamarre-Condon gave evidence about how he met Baird in October 2022 at a gay club in Sydney's inner-city.
Their relationship started of platonic and sexual, he says, but became romantic by the end of that year.
In April 2023, the accused says he went through Baird's phone and saw messages from another man.
They broke up that month, but intermittently texted and socialised, before getting back together in June 2023.
In August 2023, Lamarre-Condon testified he entered Baird's house in an attempt to go through his phone and was chased out by Baird.
He spoke about his time working with a NSW Police youth command in 2021, including allegations of homophobia and bullying.
Come November 2023, he testified he was hanging out with Baird "four to five" times a week and Baird cut him a key to his Paddington share house.
That same month, their relationship imploded over an Instagram Story Lamarre-Condon posted to bait a man he believed was also dating Baird.
He says he poured water into Baird's petrol tank in a "tit-for-tat" for scratches on his Tesla, and claims he "tried to avoid" the suburb Baird lived in.
We also heard the context for a "help me hide a body" comment Lamarre-Condon made to a friend, which he says was made while helping her recite lines while acting.
The accused discussed his mental health and suicide ideation in that period.
